opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the change will be both more mundane and more profound than people expect.

On the mundane side, a lot of a chemist's day is spent on things that aren't really chemistry: searching literature, figuring out which reaction conditions have been tried before, setting up simulations, babysitting a DFT calculation that takes three days to converge. AI is going to compress a lot of that. Language models that can read the literature and propose synthesis routes, and machine-learned force fields that give you near quantum-accurate energies at a tiny fraction of the cost, will turn what used to be weeks of work into hours. That alone changes the rhythm of research.

The more profound part is that we're starting to close the loop. For a long time, computational chemistry and experimental chemistry were two cultures that talked to each other occasionally. Now you can have a generative model propose candidate molecules or materials, a surrogate model screen them, a robotic lab synthesize and test the promising ones, and the results feed straight back into the model. That's essentially active learning or Bayesian optimization running on the physical world. Over five years I expect those self-driving labs to go from showcase demos to something a mid-sized company or a well-funded academic group can actually run.

What that does to the chemist's role, I think, is push it up a level of abstraction. You'll spend less time being the hands and more time being the person who decides what question is worth asking: what property do we actually care about, what constraints matter for manufacturability or toxicity, when is the model extrapolating into territory where it shouldn't be trusted. Chemical intuition doesn't become less valuable. It becomes the scarce resource that steers a very powerful search engine.

And I'd add a note of caution. These models are only as good as the data, and chemistry data is sparse, noisy, and heavily biased toward successful reactions, since people rarely publish failures. So one of the big shifts I'd love to see is the community treating negative results and well-curated experimental data as first-class scientific output. If we get that right, the next five years could look less like incremental improvement and more like a genuine acceleration in how fast we can discover things like better catalysts, battery materials, or carbon capture sorbents, problems where frankly we can't afford to go slowly.

r001.rationale: The response expects chemists to spend less time on routine work but still decide which questions matter, assess constraints, and judge when models are unreliable—communicating that AI will not fully automate their work within five years.

r002.rationale: It describes AI models and self-driving labs as powerful aids that accelerate research, with chemists steering the search and applying their intuition.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the change will be less dramatic than the headlines suggest and more profound than most chemists currently expect.

Let me start with what I think won't happen. I don't believe that in five years we'll have an AI that you simply ask, "give me a molecule that cures this disease," and it hands you a compound that works. Chemistry is stubbornly physical. The bottleneck is not ideas, it's verification. You still have to make the thing, purify it, characterize it, and test it, and that is slow, expensive, and often fails for reasons nobody fully understands. No amount of language modeling changes the laws of thermodynamics or the fact that a reaction that looks beautiful on paper gives you a brown sludge in the flask.

What I do think changes is the loop between hypothesis and experiment. Right now a medicinal chemist might sit down, draw a few dozen candidates based on intuition and some docking scores, pick a handful, and send them to synthesis. That intuition is wonderful but it's also very narrow, shaped by what that one person happened to see in their career. Generative models trained on large chemical and structural datasets can propose candidates from a much wider region of chemical space, and more importantly, they can be conditioned on multiple constraints at once: binding, solubility, toxicity, synthesizability. So the chemist's role shifts from generating candidates to curating and interrogating them. I think of it as the chemist becoming more of an editor than an author, at least for the first draft.

The second piece, which I'm personally very excited about, is simulation. Density functional theory has been the workhorse for decades, but it's expensive, and the accuracy is not always where you'd like it. Machine-learned force fields and neural network approximations to quantum mechanics are now getting to the point where you can run molecular dynamics at close to quantum accuracy at a tiny fraction of the cost. That means you can actually simulate reactions, catalysts, materials under realistic conditions, with solvent, at finite temperature, over timescales that matter. And this feeds back into the generative side: if your simulator is fast and accurate, you can use it as the reward signal in a closed loop. That's where the field really starts to compound.

The third piece is the lab itself. Self-driving labs, robotic synthesis, automated characterization. These exist today but they're mostly demonstrations. Over five years I expect them to become much more routine in pharma and materials companies, because the moment your model can propose and your simulator can filter, the experiment becomes the bottleneck and there's enormous economic pressure to automate it. Active learning becomes the natural organizing principle: the model decides which experiment is most informative, the robot runs it, the result updates the model.

So what does the chemist actually do in that world? I think they become much more of a scientist in the classical sense and less of a technician. Less time on the routine synthesis and more time asking which questions are worth answering, interpreting surprising results, understanding mechanism. The machine can propose and even test, but the machine has no idea what's interesting. Deciding what's interesting is still very much a human job.

I'll add one caveat, because I think it's important. There's a real risk of what I'd call the Jupyter notebook problem: tools that are powerful enough to produce results but opaque enough that the user doesn't understand what went wrong when they fail. Chemists will need a certain literacy in these models, not to build them, but to know when to trust them. Models trained on published reactions have seen almost exclusively successes, because nobody publishes the failures. That's a huge bias. So a good chemist in 2031 is someone who knows the chemistry deeply and also knows the failure modes of the tools. That combination is going to be very valuable, and honestly, it's quite rare today.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will not simply deliver a working molecule and keeps human chemists responsible for choosing questions, interpreting results, and understanding tool failures.

r002.rationale: It describes generative models, faster simulations, and lab automation expanding what chemists can do, while framing them as tools chemists must curate and understand.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change will be in the loop between designing a molecule and testing it. A chemist has some property they want—a certain activity, stability, or solubility—and AI can help propose candidates and decide which experiments are most informative. You test those candidates, feed the results back into the model, and repeat.

But proposing a molecule is only part of the problem. Can you actually synthesize it? Does it behave as expected in the real environment? Those questions make the connection to experiments essential. A model can be very convincing and still be wrong, so knowing when it is uncertain is going to matter enormously.

Over the next five years, I expect chemists to spend less time searching through possibilities and more time deciding what to pursue and interpreting the results. The exciting prospect is that they can explore ideas that would previously have been too expensive to test. I see that as a very productive partnership between chemical intuition, machine learning, and the laboratory.

r001.rationale: The response expects chemists to keep deciding what to pursue, interpreting results, and partnering with the laboratory, so it does not predict full automation within five years.

r002.rationale: It describes AI helping propose candidates and choose informative experiments, but does not clearly characterize AI as becoming increasingly powerful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change will be in the loop between proposing a molecule and finding out whether it actually does what you want. Today, that loop can be quite slow and expensive. AI can help chemists explore a much larger space of candidates and decide which experiments are most informative.

But predicting a property is only part of the problem. Can you synthesize the molecule? Is it stable? Does it behave as expected under real experimental conditions? Those constraints have to enter the model, and that requires a close connection between machine learning and chemistry.

Over the next five years, I expect more of a collaboration: the chemist brings scientific understanding and sets the questions, while the AI proposes candidates, approximates expensive calculations, and helps choose the next experiment. The exciting possibility is that you don’t just make the existing workflow faster—you can investigate questions that were previously too expensive to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response expects chemists to continue setting questions and contributing scientific understanding while AI assists, communicating that AI will not fully automate their work in the next five years.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI helping with candidate exploration, calculations, and experiment selection, but does not characterize it as becoming increasingly powerful.
